articles.title: How a community-led campaign is helping save Nigeria’s Kam language
articles.summary: The current number of Kam speakers is approximately 8,000 – 11,000. Like many other languages in northeastern Nigeria, Kam received no attention from researchers before 2016.
articles.content:
What if the most effective way to combat language endangerment is to empower community members to document their own languages? The Kam Language Project is an example of how community-led efforts can help preserve endangered languages.

Kam (also known as Nyingwom) is a language spoken in 29 villages in the Bali Local Government Area of Taraba State in Nigeria. There are an estimated 8,000–11,000 Kam language speakers today. Like many other Indigenous languages in northeastern Nigeria, Kam received no attention from researchers before 2016. As a result, there was no written literature, dictionary, standardized orthography, or audiovisual recordings of the language that could be used for documentation and preservation.

To preserve this language, Dr. Jakob Lesage, a linguist and lecturer at the Institute of Asia and African Studies, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, started the Kam Language Project in 2016. Over ten years, he worked alongside Kam community members using what he calls a “decentralized” approach: Rather than parachuting in as an outside expert, he trained a language documentation team comprising 14 members of the Kam community. At the completion of the ten-year project in March 2026, the team had produced grammar reference material for the Kam language, a digital Kam dictionary, 307 recordings (audio and video), and a website dedicated to the Kam language.

Speaking to Global Voices’ Abdulrosheed Fadipe via WhatsApp, Lesage shared the story behind the documentation project.

GV: What first drew you to work on Nigerian languages?

JL: Nigeria has a striking combination of enormous linguistic diversity, major gaps in documentation, and communities who want their languages studied and represented. About half of Nigeria’s 500-plus languages have never received serious scientific attention – the highest proportion of undocumented languages anywhere in Africa. For a linguist, the work is urgent and exciting. Studying a single undocumented language properly can overturn what we thought we knew about language classification, history, and even linguistics more generally. Kam was exactly that kind of discovery — it belongs to the Niger-Congo family, but beyond that it doesn’t fit neatly into any known subgroup, raising questions of how it arrived where it is. And it has some unusual grammatical features that can shed light on broader linguistic debates. Beyond the science, the work is meaningful to the speakers of the languages, who want their history recorded and their languages preserved. Nigeria is one of those rare places where linguistics is both scientifically important and genuinely meaningful for the people who speak the languages — people want to document their languages.

GV: Where does Kam sit on a language endangerment scale — is it under immediate threat?

JL: Kam is still actively spoken, so it’s not in crisis — but like many languages in the area, it’s under real pressure. Language loss is never just about language. A language lives in the contexts where it’s used. When those contexts disappear, the language starts to slip too. Take farming: Most Kam people are traditionally farmers. They use their language when they work the land, process crops, and trade with neighbors. But if people leave for the city — drawn by a centralized economy or pushed by unpredictable weather that makes farming difficult — those contexts vanish. New ones take their place, and those new contexts run on different languages. Move to Jalingo, the state capital, and you’ll find yourself speaking more Hausa simply because that’s what daily life there demands. As lifestyles shift, so do languages. And with roads now linking Kam villages to larger economic centers, that kind of shift could happen fast. So I’d describe Kam as locally stable but vulnerable. The crucial thing is that we’re documenting it while it's still in active, everyday use — and that's exactly what the past ten years have been about.

GV: How do you navigate the ethics of documenting a language that is not your own? And what role did native speakers play in shaping the documentation?

JL: For me, it’s important that the community isn’t just involved, but that they’re in charge of what gets documented and how. Over time, I’ve moved toward what I call a decentralized fieldwork model: The researcher isn’t the sole expert or decision-maker. Skills, equipment, and authority are shared between community collaborators. The linguist plays a supporting role. In practice, that meant Kam team members were central at every stage — recording, transcription, translation, and crucially, deciding what was worth preserving in the first place: Oral histories, local knowledge, culturally important stories. The documentation reflects what the community team considered valuable. I should be honest, though: Academic structures don’t always make this easy. There’s still strong pressure toward short-term outputs and purely theoretical results. Much of linguistics prioritizes research questions over anything directly valuable to language communities. But the field is shifting, and more projects are trying to build models where high-quality research and community priorities don’t have to pull in opposite directions. My goal is to design workflows where communities have real ownership and where the work still holds local value long after the project ends. And I’d argue that our theoretical work also stands to gain enormously from deeper partnerships with the people whose languages they study. Everyone benefits when the relationship is built right.

A community member who served as the language documentation coordinator, Babangida Audu, shared how the project started:

When the white man [Lesage] came to Sarkin Dawa in 2016, he started going to elders in the community, one of whom was my father. So he asked my father if he had an educated child who he could work with and that was how I was contacted by my father to come back home because then I was in Abuja. By the time I came back we had meetings with the white man where I helped him in transcription and translation. I joined the project because I wanted my language to move forward. Later on I was made to serve as the language documentation coordinator. We later went on to recruit others and created six teams of two individuals per team making a total of 12 people.

He added:



We communicated in English. It took a while to get used to the way he speaks. We had to demonstrate sometimes for him to understand better. He was always ready to learn. If he does not understand anything, he always asks for a better explanation.

Another team member, Garba Rahab Precious, believes the project has helped to preserve the language for generations to come, and this was made possible by working together with the community members.

The project crew were trained to use cameras for videos and audio recordings, while I was trained on how to transcribe and translate the meaning to English. On a typical day of documentation, we go to Kam villages and interview native speakers on different topics. The recorded videos will be sent to Yakub [Lesage] who will check it and we will transcribe and translate it.

GV: What challenges did you face while carrying out this project, and how did you resolve them?

JL: The biggest was COVID-19. I had planned to travel to Nigeria — and suddenly that was impossible. It forced a useful reflection for the whole field of descriptive linguistics. We rely heavily on outside researchers physically traveling to communities. The pandemic exposed how fragile that model is. It also confirmed something I’d been moving toward anyway: If community members have the skills and equipment to document their own language, the work doesn’t stop when a foreign researcher can’t get on a plane. So we pivoted to remote training. Working with Elisha Yunana — someone from a nearby community with hands-on documentation experience — we ran a two-week training for an initial Kam team of around ten people, teaching them to use the recording equipment themselves. Getting that equipment there was its own puzzle: My university had no system for purchasing it locally in Nigeria, so I bought it in Germany and relied on friends who happened to be traveling to waybill it to the Kam community. File-sharing was another headache. Audio and video files are large, and internet connections in the villages were unreliable. We solved it by routing uploads through people based in Jalingo, where connectivity was more stable. Transcription posed a different kind of challenge: Kam has no writing system. The approach that worked best was trusting speaker intuitions — starting from how people naturally represented sounds and working through readability problems as they came up, rather than imposing a system from the outside. The team rose to every one of these challenges and what we accomplished together is something I’m really proud of!

GV: If this language were to disappear tomorrow, what do you think the world would lose?

JL: The Kam world would lose a lot: Jokes, stories, how people express their relationships to one another, a way to keep things secret from people who don’t speak the language. For the rest of the world, it would mean losing a window on human culture and language that we haven't fully been able to open yet.

Lesage believes the ownership of the linguistic heritage belongs to the Kam community and also said that the materials created are, and will continue to be, accessible to everyone.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful, community-led effort to preserve the endangered Kam language in Nigeria, empowering local people to document their own linguistic heritage. This has broad cultural significance, helps safeguard human rights related to cultural identity, and provides a valuable model for language preservation worldwide. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights tangible outputs and community impact.
articles.personality_title: Community efforts help save Nigeria’s Kam language from disappearing
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Kam is a language spoken by about 8,000 to 11,000 people in 29 villages in northeastern Nigeria. Before 2016, no researchers had studied Kam, so there were no books, dictionaries, or recordings to help keep the language alive.

**What happened**
In 2016, Dr. Jakob Lesage, a linguist from Germany, started the Kam Language Project to preserve the language. Instead of working alone, he trained 14 Kam community members to record and document their own language. Over ten years, they created grammar guides, a digital dictionary, more than 300 audio and video recordings, and a website about Kam.

**Impact**
This project is special because the Kam people themselves led the work. They decided what stories and traditions to save, making sure the language reflects their culture. The project also showed that teaching local people to document their language can keep the work going, even when outside researchers cannot visit. This helps protect Kam as daily life and languages change.

**What's next step**
The materials made will stay available to everyone, helping future generations learn and use Kam. The project’s approach may inspire other communities with endangered languages to take charge of preserving their own stories and words.

**One-sentence takeaway**
By training Kam speakers to document their language, a community-led project is creating lasting tools to keep Kam alive and strong for the future.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
Le kam est une langue parlée par environ 8 000 à 11 000 personnes dans 29 villages du nord-est du Nigeria. Avant 2016, aucun chercheur ne l’avait étudiée, il n’existait donc aucun livre, dictionnaire ou enregistrement pour aider à préserver cette langue.

Les ressources créées resteront accessibles à tous, aidant les futures générations à apprendre et utiliser le Kam. Cette méthode pourrait inspirer d’autres communautés avec des langues en danger à préserver leurs propres histoires et mots.

articles.title: Identity beyond citizenship: What remains when the state refuses to recognise you?
articles.summary: Documents can confirm a legal relationship with a state, but they cannot create or erase a person’s existence, history, family, or sense of belonging.
articles.content:
This essay was written by Albert Ioffe, Jawad Fairooz, and Aleksejs Ivashuk of the Apatride Network. This post is part of Global Voices’ July 2026 Spotlight series, “Statelessness.” This series offers insight into the issue of statelessness and how it hinders people’s freedom of movement, educational opportunities, political access, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

At the end of March 2026, stateless-led organisation Apatride Network, with funding support from the organisation Porticus, facilitated a three-day gathering in Malta called Hearing and Healing. In that event, people from different stateless communities came together to share experiences and reflect collectively on the personal and collective dimensions of statelessness. The participant-led gathering moved beyond formal discussions to centre lived experience as a crucial centrepiece for unpacking and understanding statelessness. Those involved listened closely to one another, found common ground across different histories, and began shaping shared goals for future advocacy and impact.

Among the many profound discussions during the event, the following key question was covered: How do we define our identity and cultural belonging when states systematically exclude us and deny us citizenship for political, religious, ethnic, or other such arbitrary reasons? This article focuses on answering this question from the reflections of several participants of Hearing and Healing.

For many people, citizenship is an invisible part of everyday life. It is assumed rather than questioned. It provides legal recognition, freedom of movement, employment and education rights, political participation, and a sense of security, among many other rights and protections. Only when citizenship is denied does one begin to understand how profoundly it shapes the relationship between a person and the state.

Due to the unpredictability of political winds and the imperfections of governance, no state can ever truly guarantee the inviolability of legal membership in the state and the corresponding rights, no matter the factual belonging. Statelessness can suddenly happen to anyone, anywhere, at any time.

For stateless people, or those arbitrarily denied citizenship, identity becomes something that exists in constant tension. A person may have been born in a country, have ancestry on its territory, speak its language, celebrate its traditions, and contribute to its society for an entire lifetime, yet still be suddenly told that they do not legally belong. This contradiction creates one of the deepest wounds of statelessness: the separation between lived belonging and formal legal recognition.

During our Hearing and Healing gathering in Malta, participants from different countries shared remarkably similar experiences despite their diverse backgrounds. Many spoke of growing up feeling connected to their communities while simultaneously facing legal barriers that questioned their place in society. The conversations revealed that statelessness is not simply the absence of a passport. It is the experience of having one’s existence continuously challenged by administrative systems that fail or refuse to acknowledge who you are.

When governments deny citizenship for systemic reasons, people often respond by strengthening community institutions, preserving language and traditions, documenting their history, and maintaining networks across borders. These acts are not merely cultural practices; they are affirmations of existence in the face of exclusion. Their power should not be underestimated.

Statelessness is not only a legal condition — it can also become an attempt to erase history and belonging. Yet identity is shaped by many overlapping factors that exist independently of citizenship. Family, language, shared memories, cultural traditions, and collective history cannot simply be revoked by an administrative decision. Attempts to do so lead to the origins of totalitarianism and a threat to the freedom and security of everyone, whether currently impacted or not.

Throughout our discussions, it became clear that healing begins when these experiences of statelessness and erasure are acknowledged and shared. Many participants spoke openly for the first time with others who truly understood what it means to live in legal uncertainty. While every personal story was unique, they all reflected the same underlying reality: states may define legal status, but they cannot fully determine who people are. Ultimately, states possess significant power over legal status and practicability of rights, but they do not have absolute authority over principles, identity, or belonging. Those emerge from lived experience, shared history, culture, genuine dialogues, individual self-understanding, and mutual recognition.

Imposition of statelessness is by nature and definition divisive and destabilising: it fragments the social fabric and membership of society that make up the edifice on which the state is built and depends. Statelessness creates a painful contradiction for the affected: a person may belong deeply to a place culturally and historically while lacking the legal right to belong there. Recognising this contradiction is essential if societies are to understand the human cost of exclusion and work toward more inclusive systems that respect both legal rights and human dignity.

Our meeting in Malta reminded us that while statelessness isolates individuals, sharing our stories reconnects us and helps us to clear up the haze surrounding it. It transforms invisible experiences into collective understanding and reminds us that identity is ultimately defined not only by the documents we hold, but by the lives we have lived and the communities to which we truly belong.

Citizenship and even nationality should never determine whether a person’s identity is considered valid or possible. Documents can confirm a legal relationship with a state, but they cannot create or erase a person’s existence, history, family, or sense of belonging. For the many millions of stateless people around the world, the struggle is not only for a passport. It is for recognition that they have always existed, always belonged, and always deserved to be seen as full members of the societies and territory they call home.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a meaningful and inspiring event where stateless individuals come together to share experiences and advocate for recognition and belonging, addressing a significant human rights issue affecting millions globally. It provides substantial context about the challenges of statelessness and the collective efforts toward healing and inclusion, which has broad societal relevance and positive impact.
articles.personality_title: Stateless people share stories to find identity beyond citizenship
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Statelessness means not having citizenship in any country. This affects millions of people worldwide, limiting their rights and sense of belonging. In March 2026, an event called Hearing and Healing brought together stateless people from different countries to talk about their experiences.

**What happened** – The Apatride Network, a group led by stateless people, organized a three-day meeting in Malta with support from Porticus. Participants shared personal stories about living without citizenship and discussed how this affects their identity and place in society. They focused on how legal systems deny them recognition, even though they belong to communities by culture, language, and family.

**Impact** – The event showed that citizenship is more than a document—it shapes everyday life in many ways. Stateless people often feel deeply connected to their homes but are legally excluded. By sharing their stories, they built understanding and support among themselves, showing that identity comes from lived experience, not just official papers. This gathering helped heal some of the pain caused by exclusion and inspired ideas for future advocacy.

**What's next step** – The participants plan to use what they learned to push for better recognition and rights for stateless people. Their shared experiences will help raise awareness and encourage governments to create fairer systems that respect both legal status and human dignity.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Stateless people’s stories reveal that identity and belonging go beyond legal citizenship and are shaped by culture, history, and community.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les apatrides partagent leurs histoires pour trouver une identité au-delà de la citoyenneté
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

Les participants ont partagé des histoires personnelles sur la vie sans citoyenneté et ont discuté de l’impact sur leur identité et leur place dans la société. Ils ont expliqué comment les systèmes juridiques les excluent malgré leur attachement culturel, linguistique et familial.

**Impact** – L’événement a montré que la citoyenneté est plus qu’un document : elle influence la vie quotidienne de nombreuses façons. Les apatrides se sentent souvent profondément liés à leur pays, mais sont exclus légalement. En partageant leurs histoires, ils ont créé du soutien et montré que l’identité vient de l’expérience vécue, pas seulement des papiers officiels. Cette rencontre a aidé à guérir une partie de la douleur liée à cette exclusion et a inspiré des idées pour l’avenir.

**Prochaine étape** – Les participants prévoient d’utiliser ce qu’ils ont appris pour défendre une meilleure reconnaissance et plus de droits pour les apatrides. Leurs récits aideront à sensibiliser et à encourager les gouvernements à créer des systèmes plus justes qui respectent le statut légal et la dignité humaine.

articles.personality_title_es: Personas apátridas comparten historias para encontrar identidad más allá de la ciudadanía

articles.title: How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
articles.summary: Discipline at an academy trust went too far - parents, pupils and former teachers tell BBC Panorama.
articles.content:
To avoid getting into trouble at school, 14-year-old Amelia says she decided to stop drinking water so she would not need the toilet.

Her school, Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall, had introduced strict disciplinary policies, which included limiting toilet visits during classes, according to pupils and former teachers.

New discipline rules were implemented when the school was taken over in January 2024 by the Athena Learning Trust, which runs six secondary schools in Devon and Cornwall.

Amelia's mother, Kayley, believes these strict policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill from a series of serious infections caused by not drinking.

Hundreds of parents, including Kayley, have campaigned against the way Athena run its schools - and their vocal opposition now appears to have paid off. Last month, the trust announced it was planning to disband and transfer all its schools to other trusts.

It said that trustees had "listened carefully to feedback" and recognised the "clear need for change".

BBC Panorama has spoken to nearly 100 pupils, parents and former teachers from Athena schools, who say levels of discipline went too far. Many pupils and parents queued to talk to us at two town hall meetings we arranged.

The way the schools had been run was "authoritarian" and "cruel", some said.

"You're constantly scared you're going to do something wrong," one student with ADHD told us, while a former music teacher said the strict discipline had meant his lessons were taught in silence.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a successful community campaign by parents, pupils, and former teachers against overly strict and harmful school disciplinary policies. The campaign led to the disbanding of the academy trust responsible and promises of change, representing a meaningful victory for student welfare and rights in education. The story has broad social significance and clear positive impact on children's health and wellbeing.
articles.personality_title: Parents and pupils challenge strict school rules and win change
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In early 2024, the Athena Learning Trust took over several schools in southwest England, including Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall. They introduced tough new discipline rules, like limiting toilet breaks during lessons.

**What happened** – Many students, parents, and former teachers spoke out against these harsh rules. Fourteen-year-old Amelia stopped drinking water to avoid needing the toilet, which made her sick. Hundreds of parents joined a campaign to protest the strict policies. After listening to this feedback, Athena decided to close down and hand over its schools to other trusts.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows how a community can work together to stop rules that harm students’ health and well-being. The campaign helped protect children from unfair discipline and brought attention to the need for kinder school environments.

**What’s next step** – The schools will be managed by new trusts, which will hopefully create better rules that respect students’ needs. Parents and teachers will likely keep watching to make sure changes really happen.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A strong community effort successfully ended harmful school discipline and opened the door for kinder, healthier learning environments.
articles.personality_title_fr: Parents et élèves s'opposent aux règles strictes de l'école et obtiennent des changements
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au début de 2024, le Athena Learning Trust a pris en charge plusieurs écoles dans le sud-ouest de l’Angleterre, dont le Camborne Science and International Academy en Cornouailles. **Ce qui s’est passé** – De nombreux élèves, parents et anciens enseignants se sont opposés à ces règles strictes. Amelia, 14 ans, a arrêté de boire de l’eau pour éviter d’avoir besoin d’aller aux toilettes, ce qui l’a rendue malade. Des centaines de parents ont lancé une campagne pour protester contre ces politiques. Après avoir écouté ces retours, Athena a décidé de fermer et de transférer ses écoles à d’autres organismes.

**Impact** – Cela montre qu’une communauté peut s’unir pour arrêter des règles qui nuisent à la santé et au bien-être des élèves. La campagne a aidé à protéger les enfants contre une discipline injuste et a souligné l’importance d’un environnement scolaire plus bienveillant.

**Prochaine étape** – Les écoles seront gérées par de nouveaux organismes, qui espèrent créer de meilleures règles respectant les besoins des élèves. Les parents et enseignants continueront probablement à surveiller pour s’assurer que les changements se réalisent.

**En résumé** – Un fort effort communautaire a permis de mettre fin à une discipline scolaire nuisible et a ouvert la voie à un environnement d’apprentissage plus sain et plus humain.

**Contexto** – A principios de 2024, el Athena Learning Trust tomó el control de varias escuelas en el suroeste de Inglaterra, incluyendo la Camborne Science and International Academy en Cornwall. Introdujeron reglas disciplinarias estrictas, como limitar las visitas al baño durante las clases.

**Qué pasó** – Muchos estudiantes, padres y exprofesores protestaron contra estas reglas duras. Amelia, de 14 años, dejó de beber agua para no tener que ir al baño, lo que le causó problemas de salud. Cientos de padres iniciaron una campaña para oponerse a estas políticas. Tras escuchar estas opiniones, Athena decidió cerrar y transferir sus escuelas a otros organismos.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque muestra cómo una comunidad puede unirse para detener reglas que dañan la salud y el bienestar de los estudiantes. La campaña ayudó a proteger a los niños de una disciplina injusta y resaltó la necesidad de ambientes escolares más amables.

**Próximo paso** – Las escuelas serán gestionadas por nuevos organismos, que esperan crear reglas mejores que respeten las necesidades de los estudiantes. Probablemente, padres y profesores seguirán atentos para asegurar que los cambios se cumplan.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un esfuerzo comunitario fuerte logró acabar con una disciplina escolar dañina y abrió la puerta a ambientes de aprendizaje más saludables y humanos.

articles.title: Trapped by a Facebook job advert, freed by a stranger in a taxi
articles.summary: Sofia* was 27, raising her seven-year-old son alone in Venezuela, and running out of options. For years she had distributed personal hygiene products door to door, but as her customers’ finances collapsed, so did her income.
articles.content:
Debts piled up. Eventually she had no choice but to quit and start looking for something else.

That is when she saw the advert on Facebook Marketplace: a job in Trinidad and Tobago, all expenses paid, work waiting on arrival.

© Unsplash/Renaldo Matamoro

A woman calling herself “Valentina” messaged her on WhatsApp. They spoke by phone. The offer sounded real because Valentina sounded real.

“We spoke directly,” Sofia recalls. “I heard her voice. I believed it was real.”

The truth unfolds

Sofia had no way of knowing that Valentina was part of a trafficking network. She boarded a flight to Trinidad and Tobago believing a new life awaited her.

It did not take long for that belief to collapse. The people who met her at her destination were not the people she had spoken to. Whatever she had been promised evaporated. Sofia had been trafficked for sexual exploitation.

“I was kidnapped and forced to do what they told me to do,” she says.

For weeks she lived under the control of her captors, in constant fear. At one point, they pushed her to help recruit other Venezuelan women using the same false promises that had trapped her. It was a line she would not cross.

“I didn’t want other people to go through what I went through,” she says.

An ordinary day, an extraordinary chance

Sofia prefers not to dwell on those weeks now. “I buried that time,” she says. But one day she is willing to revisit, because it changed everything.

She was sent outside to take out the garbage – and saw her opening. She packed a few belongings, slipped out, and got into a taxi.

Another passenger was already inside: a Dominican woman who had lived in Trinidad and Tobago for years and immediately sensed something was wrong. Sofia told her what was happening. Rather than turn away, the woman suggested they stop near a police station and report it. Sofia agreed.

“I felt it was God’s work,” she says.

At the police station, for the first time since she had arrived in the country, Sofia felt safe.

“That was when I felt I was finally out of it,” she says.

Rebuilding, with support

Sofia’s escape marked the beginning of a longer process, carried out in partnership between national authorities and the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM).

© IOM

Trinidad and Tobago’s Counter Trafficking Unit connected her to medical care, including forensic examinations, health screenings and counselling. She remains under their protection for the time being.

Through its long-running partnership with the Unit, IOM Trinidad and Tobago has provided survivors like Sofia with emergency food assistance, safe shelter, mental health and psychosocial support, and vocational training geared toward long-term reintegration.

The same partnership has trained counter-trafficking personnel and run public awareness campaigns to help others recognise the warning signs Sofia missed.

“Everything has been done correctly,” she says. “I have felt supported.”

Looking ahead

Sofia has since told her family in Venezuela the truth about what happened to her. Her son, now seven, remains her biggest reason to keep going. She hopes to return to education, attend university and build a stable career – and a secure future for them both.

She is also determined that her story might spare someone else the same ordeal.

“Not everything is real,” she says of opportunities advertised online, urging others to ask questions and verify before they travel. “I don’t want what happened to me to happen to anyone else.”

Even in her darkest moments, she says, she held onto belief. “You have to have faith in yourself.”

Asked what she is most proud of, she does not hesitate: “Having the courage to escape. I am a strong woman. I was able to get out.”

The World Day Against Trafficking in Persons is marked annually on 30 July.

*Name changed to protect identity.
